finding.title: `err :=` shadows the outer err, so gzip write and close errors are dropped

other.title: gzip writer is not closed when writeEntries fails

findings.title: `err :=` shadows the outer err, so gzip write and close errors are dropped
findings.scenario: With -gzip, the destination returns an error, for example disk full. The inner `err` holds it and goes out of scope. `Write` returns the outer `err`, which is still nil. main treats the export as successful, keeps the partial or corrupt file, and never runs the remove-on-failure path.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The compiler accepts the shadowing because the inner err is used. No test covers a failing writer with Gzip enabled. `go vet` does not flag shadowing by default.

findings.title: gzip writer is not closed when writeEntries fails
findings.scenario: If writeEntries fails, compressed.Close() is skipped. The caller deletes the file anyway, so the effect is small, but the writer is left unclosed.
findings.whyNotPrevented: No test covers this path.

finding.title: Shadowed err in gzip branch drops all write and close errors

findings.title: Shadowed err in gzip branch drops all write and close errors
findings.scenario: With -gzip, the disk fills or the writer fails. The inner `err :=` declares a new variable scoped to the if block. `Write` returns the outer `err`, which is still nil. main sees success, so it does not remove the partial file and it reports no error. That leaves a truncated gzip file behind, which is the opposite of what was asked.
findings.whyNotPrevented: Go allows the shadowing. The compiler does not flag it because the inner err is used. No test covers gzip with a failing writer.

finding.title: Shadowed err makes gzip write errors get swallowed

findings.title: Shadowed err makes gzip write errors get swallowed
findings.scenario: With -gzip, if the underlying file write fails (disk full, closed file), the inner `err :=` declares a new variable in the if block. The outer `err` stays nil, so Write returns nil. main then reports success and keeps a truncated or corrupt .gz file.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The compiler allows the shadowing because the inner err is used. No test covers a failing writer with Gzip set. go vet does not flag shadowing by default.

finding.title: Length truncated to u16 while the limit still allows 256 KiB messages

findings.title: Length truncated to u16 while the limit still allows 256 KiB messages
findings.scenario: A 70,000-byte message passes the MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES check (262144). `as u16` truncates the length to 4464, so the header is wrong. The decoder then returns a 4464-byte message and treats the remaining bytes as the start of the next frame. This corrupts the stream silently.
findings.whyNotPrevented: MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES in src/limits.rs is still 256 * 1024. The only oversize test uses MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES + 1, and no test covers a message between 65536 and 262144 bytes.
findings.measuredBy: Grep MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES: src/limits.rs:2 = 256 * 1024; src/frame.rs:12 checks only against that

finding.title: Length cast to u16 truncates messages above 65535 bytes, but the size limit is still 256 KiB

findings.title: Length cast to u16 truncates messages above 65535 bytes, but the size limit is still 256 KiB
findings.scenario: A 70,000-byte message passes the `> MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES` check (262144). `as u16` writes 70000 mod 65536 = 4464 as the length. The full 70,000 bytes follow. The decoder reads a 4464-byte frame and treats the remaining bytes as the start of the next frame. The stream is corrupted and messages are lost or misparsed, with no error.
findings.whyNotPrevented: MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES in src/limits.rs is `256 * 1024`, far above u16::MAX. `as` casts truncate silently. No test covers a message between 65536 and the limit.
findings.measuredBy: Grep MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES: src/limits.rs:2 `pub const MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES: usize = 256 * 1024;`

findings.title: Lambdas in loop all capture the last limit, so title and summary are limited to 5000
findings.scenario: The lambda reads `limit` when it is called, not when it is defined. After the loop `limit` is 5000, so all three validators use 5000. A title of 100 characters passes validate(), although the title limit is 80. A summary of 1000 characters passes too.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The only new test checks a body of 5001 characters, which fails under any limit. No test checks a title or summary over its limit. The existing test uses short strings.

findings.title: SplitHostPort error fallback for RemoteAddr
findings.scenario: net/http always sets RemoteAddr as host:port for TCP connections, so the error branch is unlikely to run. It could matter for unix sockets or custom listeners, which this change does not show are used.

finding.title: Trailing windows leave out the newest reading

other.title: Tests cannot detect a wrong window position

findings.title: Trailing windows leave out the newest reading
findings.scenario: With 5 readings [20,20,20,20,40] and window 5, the range 5..5 is empty, so trailing_average returns [] and should_open returns false even though the newest reading is 40. With 6 readings the last window is values[1..5], which skips values[5], the newest. The author asked for the last five readings including the newest.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The tests use constant readings, so the window position does not change the result. The too-few-readings test only covers len < window, not len == window.

findings.title: Tests cannot detect a wrong window position
findings.scenario: Constant input gives the same average for any window offset, so the off-by-one passes. No test checks that the newest value affects the result, or that len == window returns one value.
findings.whyNotPrevented: No test uses varying values.

finding.title: Window range is off by one, so the newest reading is never averaged

findings.title: Window range is off by one, so the newest reading is never averaged
findings.scenario: With window 5 and exactly 5 readings [20,20,20,20,40], `window..len` is `5..5`, which is empty. `trailing_average` returns an empty Vec, so `should_open` is false. With 6 readings the last window is `values[0..5]`, so the newest reading is left out. The author asked for the last five readings including the newest one.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The tests use constant values and only check an empty result for too few readings. None checks which readings fall in a window or that the newest one counts.

findings.title: Tests cannot detect the off-by-one
findings.scenario: A constant series gives the same averages whichever window positions are used. A test with varying values, such as [1,2,3,4] with window 2 expecting [1.5,2.5,3.5], would fail on the current code.
findings.whyNotPrevented: No test uses varying values, and none covers `should_open`.

finding.title: Trailing average leaves out the newest reading

findings.title: Trailing average leaves out the newest reading
findings.scenario: With temperatures [20,20,20,20,20,40] and window 5, `end` only reaches 5, so the last window is readings 0..5 and the 40 is never averaged in. should_open stays false (the average is 20) when it should be 24. With exactly 5 readings the range is empty, so the result is empty and the vents never open.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The new tests use constant data, which gives the same result whichever window is picked. They also only test a too-short input, not the exact-length case or whether the newest value counts.

finding.title: Mutable default argument is shared across calls and grows with every digest

findings.title: Mutable default argument is shared across calls and grows with every digest
findings.scenario: build_digest(['a']) and then build_digest(['b']) both use the same default list. The second digest's recipients are [TEAM_INBOX, TEAM_INBOX], and the Digest objects share one list. Every later call adds another copy, so the team inbox gets duplicate mail. The existing test_team_inbox_gets_the_digest asserts == [TEAM_INBOX] and fails if another test has already called build_digest without recipients.
findings.whyNotPrevented: No test calls the default path twice in a row and checks recipients. Python does not warn about mutable defaults.

findings.title: Caller's recipients list is mutated, and the digest aliases it
findings.scenario: send_weekly passes project.watchers(). If that returns a stored list, each weekly run appends TEAM_INBOX to it. The watchers list then accumulates duplicates, and the team inbox gets repeated copies of the digest. Callers who reuse a list for several digests see the same effect.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The new test passes a fresh literal list and never checks that the input is left unchanged.

findings.title: Team inbox is not de-duplicated when a caller already lists it
findings.scenario: If a project's watchers include the team inbox address, the digest lists it twice. The mailer may then send the team inbox two copies.
findings.whyNotPrevented: No check or test covers an overlap between the watchers and the team inbox.

finding.title: Mutable default list is shared and the caller's list is mutated

findings.title: Mutable default list is shared and the caller's list is mutated
findings.scenario: build_digest(['a']) twice: the shared default list gets TEAM_INBOX appended on each call, so the second digest has recipients [TEAM_INBOX, TEAM_INBOX] and the team inbox gets duplicate mails. Passing project.watchers() also appends TEAM_INBOX to the caller's list, which may be the project's stored watcher list. Each later call or weekly run adds another copy. The existing test test_team_inbox_gets_the_digest asserts [TEAM_INBOX] and fails once any earlier call has used the default.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The new test passes a fresh literal list and only one call uses the default, so the shared state is never exercised. No test calls build_digest twice without recipients.

findings.title: Mutable default argument is mutated, so the team inbox piles up across calls
findings.scenario: Call build_digest(entries) twice with no recipients. The shared default list gets TEAM_INBOX appended each time, so the second digest has recipients [TEAM_INBOX, TEAM_INBOX] and the team inbox gets duplicate mails. Test order also matters. test_subject_counts_updates calls build_digest(['a']) several times, and that grows the default list. If it runs before test_team_inbox_gets_the_digest, the assertion `recipients == [TEAM_INBOX]` fails.

findings.title: Caller's recipients list is mutated and reused inside the Digest
findings.scenario: send_weekly passes project.watchers(). If that returns a stored list, each weekly run appends TEAM_INBOX to the project's watcher list. The team inbox is then added as a watcher and repeats on every run. Because the Digest shares the same list object, later changes to it also change the digest's recipients.
findings.whyNotPrevented: The function neither copies the input nor builds a new list. No test checks that the passed list is left unchanged.
